title: Demonstrate an understanding of basic accounting practices

lessons.title: Why we keep records of money
lessons.html:
What is accounting?

Accounting means writing down all the money that comes into a business and all the money that goes out, and then checking what is left. It helps the owner see if the business is making a profit or a loss.

Even a small business, like selling eggs or vegetables, needs records. Without records you do not know if you are really making money, and you cannot prove anything to the bank or to SARS.

Income and expenses

  • Income is money that comes in, for example money from selling 20 trays of eggs.
  • Expenses are money that goes out, for example chicken feed, transport, egg trays and wages.
  • Profit = income minus expenses, when income is bigger.
  • Loss = when expenses are bigger than income.

Example

Nomsa sells eggs. In March she sells eggs for R3 200. She spends R1 900 on feed, R300 on trays and R400 on transport. Her expenses are R2 600. Her profit is R3 200 minus R2 600 = R600.

Source documents

Every amount you write down must come from proof. This proof is called a source document.

DocumentWhat it shows
InvoiceWhat a buyer owes you, or what you owe a supplier
ReceiptMoney that was paid
Till slipSomething bought at a shop
Bank statementMoney in and out of the bank account
Payslip / wage sheetWages paid to workers

Keep all slips and documents in a file or box, in order of date. Do not throw them away.

lessons.title: Keeping a simple cash book and budget
lessons.html:
The cash book

The easiest record is a cash book. It is a book or a page with columns where you write every amount of money in and out, on the day it happens.

DateDetailsMoney in (R)Money out (R)
2 MarchSold eggs to shop800
4 MarchBought 2 bags of feed950
9 MarchSold eggs at market1 200

At the end of the month you add up the money in column and the money out column. The difference tells you how much cash you gained or lost. Check the answer against the cash in your tin or the bank balance.

Good habits

  1. Write things down the same day, not at the end of the month.
  2. Keep business money separate from household money. Open a separate bank account if you can.
  3. Number your receipts and keep a copy of every receipt you give.
  4. Count your cash often and make sure it agrees with your book.
  5. Never change a figure by rubbing it out. Draw a line through the mistake and write the correct amount next to it.

A simple budget

A budget is a plan of the money you expect to get and spend in the future. Before planting a hectare of cabbages, a farmer writes down the expected cost of seedlings, fertiliser, water, labour and transport, and the expected income from sales. If the costs are higher than the income, the plan must change.

Assets and liabilities

An asset is something the business owns, such as a bakkie, a water tank or cash. A liability is money the business owes, such as a loan. Knowing both helps you see what the business is worth.

Key points

  • Accounting records all money in and out of a business.
  • Profit is income minus expenses.
  • Every entry needs a source document such as an invoice or receipt.
  • Use a cash book and write in it every day.
  • A budget is a plan for future income and spending.
